items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The 1947 US policy of supporting free peoples resisting subjugation, the start of containment"?
items.answer: Truman Doctrine
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Truman Doctrine.

items.stem: Explain the difference between capitalism and communism.
items.answer: Capitalism is based on private ownership, markets and individual freedom; communism (Soviet-style) on state ownership, central planning and one-party rule.
items.markingKey: Capitalism is based on private ownership, markets and individual freedom; communism (Soviet-style) on state ownership, central planning and one-party rule. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "The Cold War never involved real fighting." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The superpowers did not fight each other directly, but proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and elsewhere killed millions.
items.markingKey: The superpowers did not fight each other directly, but proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and elsewhere killed millions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Place these events in chronological order, earliest first: the Truman Doctrine is announced (1947 CE); the Berlin Blockade begins (1948 CE); the Potsdam Conference (1945 CE); Churchill's "iron curtain" speech at Fulton (1946 CE).
items.answer: the Potsdam Conference → Churchill's "iron curtain" speech at Fulton → the Truman Doctrine is announced → the Berlin Blockade begins
items.markingKey: the Potsdam Conference → Churchill's "iron curtain" speech at Fulton → the Truman Doctrine is announced → the Berlin Blockade begins. A larger BCE number is earlier. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark one adjacent pair swapped.

items.stem: Explain why "How far did the Marshall Plan contribute to the division of Europe between 1947 and 1949?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into the origins of the Cold War: capitalism versus communism, Yalta, Potsdam and the iron curtain.
items.answer: It examines one factor's role in a process, allowing evaluation of interpretations.
items.markingKey: It examines one factor's role in a process, allowing evaluation of interpretations. items.stem: Lukas argues that "The USSR was mainly responsible for the start of the Cold War." Isabel disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Post-revisionist historians such as John Lewis Gaddis argue that both sides contributed, though Stalin's actions and suspicion were particularly important.
items.markingKey: Lukas: Stalin imposed communist governments in Eastern Europe, breaking Yalta promises. Isabel: the USA used its economic and atomic power to extend influence. items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Who started the Cold War?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the origins of the Cold War: capitalism versus communism, Yalta, Potsdam and the iron curtain. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.

items.stem: "The USSR was mainly responsible for the start of the Cold War." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Post-revisionist historians such as John Lewis Gaddis argue that both sides contributed, though Stalin's actions and suspicion were particularly important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Stalin imposed communist governments in Eastern Europe, breaking Yalta promises; the Berlin Blockade was an aggressive act. items.stem: Explain why the Marshall Plan increased Cold War tensions.
items.answer: The USSR saw it as "dollar imperialism" to extend US influence; it forbade Eastern European states from accepting aid, deepening the division of Europe.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Yalta Conference and the Potsdam Conference.
items.answer: Yalta (February 1945) was relatively cooperative, agreeing on zones in Germany and free elections in Eastern Europe; Potsdam (July–August 1945) was tenser, with new leaders Truman and Attlee and disputes over Poland and reparations.
items.markingKey: Yalta (February 1945) was relatively cooperative, agreeing on zones in Germany and free elections in Eastern Europe; Potsdam (July–August 1945) was tenser, with new leaders Truman and Attlee and disputes over Poland and reparations. items.stem: In which century did the Potsdam Conference (1945 CE) take place?
items.answer: 20th century CE
items.markingKey: A. 1945 CE falls in the 20th century CE: e.g. the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Winston Churchill, "Sinews of Peace" speech, Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, 5 March 1946

The former British prime minister told an American audience that an iron curtain had descended across Europe from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, and that the ancient capitals behind it were increasingly under Moscow's control. He called for close cooperation between Britain and the USA.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Soviet control was dividing Europe, so Britain and the USA must stand together.
items.markingKey: Soviet control was dividing Europe, so Britain and the USA must stand together. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "38th parallel"?

A country formally independent but under the control of another, such as Poland under Soviet influence
The 1947 US policy of supporting free peoples resisting subjugation, the start of containment
Competition between the superpowers to build more and better weapons, especially nuclear weapons
items.answer: The line of latitude dividing North and South Korea after 1945
items.markingKey: A. "38th parallel" is the line of latitude dividing North and South Korea after 1945.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "The Korean War ended with a US victory." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It ended in a stalemate near the 38th parallel in 1953, with about 3 million deaths.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Berlin Blockade and the building of the Berlin Wall.
items.answer: The Blockade (1948–49) tried to force the West out of Berlin; the Wall (1961) accepted the West's presence but sealed East Berliners in.

items.stem: Arjun argues that "Containment was a successful policy for the USA between 1947 and 1962." Leila disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Containment largely succeeded in Europe, but its record in Asia and Latin America was mixed and costly.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Containment was a successful policy for the USA between 1947 and 1962." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Containment largely succeeded in Europe, but its record in Asia and Latin America was mixed and costly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it preserved West Berlin, Western Europe and South Korea; Soviet missiles were removed from Cuba. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "détente"?
options: The Soviet policy under Gorbachev of letting Eastern European states choose their own path
The 1987 US–Soviet treaty eliminating intermediate-range nuclear missiles
A conflict in which superpowers support opposing sides rather than fighting each other directly
The easing of Cold War tensions in the late 1960s and 1970s
items.answer: The easing of Cold War tensions in the late 1960s and 1970s
items.markingKey: D. "détente" is the easing of Cold War tensions in the late 1960s and 1970s.

items.markingKey: Britain (1952), France (1960) and China (1964) also developed nuclear weapons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the space race was linked to the arms race.

items.stem: With reference to the Apollo 11 Moon landing, explain how it illustrates the space race.
items.answer: On 20 July 1969 the USA landed astronauts on the Moon; an estimated 600 million people watched on television. The USA achieved a symbolic victory and showed its technological power.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "The nuclear arms race made the world safer during the Cold War."
items.answer: Thesis: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: MAD deterred direct war between the superpowers; crises such as Cuba led to arms control. Thesis/conclusion: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable. items.answer: Deterrence keeps weapons to prevent attack; disarmament reduces or eliminates weapons.
items.markingKey: Deterrence keeps weapons to prevent attack; disarmament reduces or eliminates weapons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: The Soviet people and system led humanity into space.

items.stem: Estimated stockpiles: 1960 – USA 18,638, USSR 1,605; 1970 – USA 26,008, USSR 11,643. Calculate the combined total for each year and the percentage change, and explain what the figures suggest about the arms race and détente.
items.markingKey: Totals 20,243 and 37,651 (A1 A1); change (37,651 − 20,243) ÷ 20,243 × 100 = +86% (M1 A1). Analysis (2): rapid growth shows the arms race; the USSR overtook the USA in the late 1970s; arms-control agreements (SALT) limited launchers rather than warheads, so stockpiles grew even during détente until the late 1980s.

items.stem: Define the term "Velvet Revolution".

items.stem: Briefly explain why Gorbachev's reforms helped bring down communism in Eastern Europe.

items.stem: How many years passed between Sputnik 1 is launched (1957 CE) and the Berlin Wall is built (1961 CE)?
items.answer: 4 years
items.markingKey: 4 by subtraction (M1 A1). BCE years count down towards 1 BCE; the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE.

items.stem: Sana argues that "The nuclear arms race made the world safer during the Cold War." Tomás disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable.
items.markingKey: Sana: MAD deterred direct war between the superpowers. Tomás: the world came close to nuclear war in 1962 and 1983. Judgement (1-2 marks): Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable.

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "How far did economic problems in the USSR in the 1980s cause the collapse of Soviet control in Eastern Europe in 1989?"
items.answer: It weighs economic factors against others in a major historical change.
items.markingKey: It weighs economic factors against others in a major historical change. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Winston Churchill, "Sinews of Peace" speech, Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, 5 March 1946

The former British prime minister told an American audience that an iron curtain had descended across Europe from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, and that the ancient capitals behind it were increasingly under Moscow's control. He called for close cooperation between Britain and the USA.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The USSR was mainly responsible for the start of the Cold War."
items.answer: Post-revisionist historians such as John Lewis Gaddis argue that both sides contributed, though Stalin's actions and suspicion were particularly important.
items.markingKey: From the source: Soviet control was dividing Europe, so Britain and the USA must stand together. Own knowledge for: Stalin imposed communist governments in Eastern Europe, breaking Yalta promises; the Berlin Blockade was an aggressive act. Own knowledge against: the USA used its economic and atomic power to extend influence; mutual fears and misunderstandings drove both sides. Judgement: Post-revisionist historians such as John Lewis Gaddis argue that both sides contributed, though Stalin's actions and suspicion were particularly important. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of John F. Kennedy, televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962

The US president told the nation that unmistakable evidence showed offensive missile sites were being built in Cuba. He announced a strict quarantine on all offensive military equipment shipped to Cuba and called on the Soviet leader to remove the threat.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about containment and crises: Berlin, Korea and the Cuban Missile Crisis. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of John F. Kennedy, televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962. Purpose: to inform the public, justify US action and pressure the USSR. Value: It shows the official US position and the president's public strategy. Limitation: It presents only the US perspective and does not mention US missiles in Turkey or secret negotiations.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of John F. Kennedy, televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962. Purpose: to inform the public, justify US action and pressure the USSR. Value: It shows the official US position and the president's public strategy. Limitation: It presents only the US perspective and does not mention US missiles in Turkey or secret negotiations. Award up to [4]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". items.stem: "The nuclear arms race made the world safer during the Cold War." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: MAD deterred direct war between the superpowers; crises such as Cuba led to arms control. Arguments against: the world came close to nuclear war in 1962 and 1983; enormous resources were diverted and tests harmed people and environments. Supported judgement: Deterrence may have prevented a direct superpower war, but the arms race created serious risks of catastrophe; "safer" is debatable. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Mikhail Gorbachev, address to the UN General Assembly, New York, 7 December 1988

The Soviet leader told the United Nations that force and the threat of force could no longer be instruments of foreign policy, and that every nation must have freedom of choice. He announced a unilateral reduction of Soviet armed forces by 500,000 troops.

"Gorbachev was the most important reason for the end of the Cold War." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Gorbachev was the key individual, but his choices were shaped by economic crisis and popular pressure; the end of the Cold War had several interacting causes.
items.markingKey: From the source: The USSR would not use force and would let nations choose their own path. Own knowledge for: his reforms and refusal to use force allowed peaceful change; he negotiated arms reductions such as the INF Treaty. Own knowledge against: the Soviet economy was already in deep crisis; popular movements such as Solidarity and US pressure also mattered. Judgement: Gorbachev was the key individual, but his choices were shaped by economic crisis and popular pressure; the end of the Cold War had several interacting causes. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Where did Churchill make his "iron curtain" speech in March 1946?
items.answer: Fulton, Missouri
items.markingKey: A. Truman was present.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A conflict in which superpowers support opposing sides rather than fighting each other directly"?
items.answer: proxy war
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of proxy war.

items.stem: Which was the first artificial satellite, launched by the USSR in October 1957?
items.answer: Sputnik 1
items.markingKey: Sputnik 1. It shocked the USA.

items.stem: "Gorbachev intended to end communism." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: He aimed to reform and save Soviet socialism, but his reforms unleashed forces he could not control.
items.markingKey: He aimed to reform and save Soviet socialism, but his reforms unleashed forces he could not control. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Historians agree that the USSR caused the Cold War." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Orthodox historians blamed Soviet expansion, revisionists blamed US economic imperialism, and post-revisionists stress mutual misunderstanding.
items.markingKey: Orthodox historians blamed Soviet expansion, revisionists blamed US economic imperialism, and post-revisionists stress mutual misunderstanding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the Berlin Wall was built.
items.answer: About 3 million East Germans had fled to the West through Berlin since 1949, damaging the East German economy and image; the wall stopped the exodus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: About 3 million East Germans had fled to the West through Berlin since 1949, damaging the East German economy and image; the wall stopped the exodus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between disarmament and deterrence.
items.answer: Deterrence keeps weapons to prevent attack; disarmament reduces or eliminates weapons.
items.markingKey: Deterrence keeps weapons to prevent attack; disarmament reduces or eliminates weapons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Gorbachev intended to end communism." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: He aimed to reform and save Soviet socialism, but his reforms unleashed forces he could not control.
items.markingKey: He aimed to reform and save Soviet socialism, but his reforms unleashed forces he could not control. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Germany became the centre of Cold War rivalry.
items.answer: Both sides wanted to control Germany's future and industrial power; disagreements over reparations, currency and government led to its division in 1949.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both sides wanted to control Germany's future and industrial power; disagreements over reparations, currency and government led to its division in 1949. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Place these events in chronological order, earliest first: the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963 CE); the Berlin Blockade begins (1948 CE); the Korean War begins (1950 CE); the Warsaw Pact is formed (1955 CE).
items.answer: the Berlin Blockade begins → the Korean War begins → the Warsaw Pact is formed → the Partial Test Ban Treaty
items.markingKey: the Berlin Blockade begins → the Korean War begins → the Warsaw Pact is formed → the Partial Test Ban Treaty. A larger BCE number is earlier. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark one adjacent pair swapped.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the arms race, the space race and Cold War propaganda?
options: How did the launch of Sputnik in 1957 influence US education and science policy?
items.answer: How did the launch of Sputnik in 1957 influence US education and science policy?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: In which century did the INF Treaty (1987 CE) take place?
items.answer: 20th century CE
items.markingKey: A. 1987 CE falls in the 20th century CE: e.g. the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the Marshall Plan increased Cold War tensions.
items.answer: The USSR saw it as "dollar imperialism" to extend US influence; it forbade Eastern European states from accepting aid, deepening the division of Europe.
items.markingKey: Content: The USSR saw it as "dollar imperialism" to extend US influence; it forbade Eastern European states from accepting aid, deepening the division of Europe. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Poster (described): Soviet propaganda poster celebrating Yuri Gagarin's flight, published by the state publisher, Moscow, 1961

A Soviet poster from 1961 shows a smiling cosmonaut in a helmet with the letters of the USSR, a rocket rising behind him, and a slogan celebrating the glory of the Soviet people who opened the way to space.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching the arms race, the space race and Cold War propaganda? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Soviet propaganda poster celebrating Yuri Gagarin's flight, published by the state publisher, Moscow, 1961. Purpose: to celebrate the achievement and promote pride in the Soviet system. Value: It shows how the USSR used space success to promote communism. Limitation: It is state propaganda that hides failures and costs of the space programme.
items.markingKey: Origin: Soviet propaganda poster celebrating Yuri Gagarin's flight, published by the state publisher, Moscow, 1961. Purpose: to celebrate the achievement and promote pride in the Soviet system. Value: It shows how the USSR used space success to promote communism. Limitation: It is state propaganda that hides failures and costs of the space programme. Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Mikhail Gorbachev, address to the UN General Assembly, New York, 7 December 1988

The Soviet leader told the United Nations that force and the threat of force could no longer be instruments of foreign policy, and that every nation must have freedom of choice. He announced a unilateral reduction of Soviet armed forces by 500,000 troops.

According to Source A, what can we learn about the end of the Cold War and the fall of the Berlin Wall? Support your answer with details from the source.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How far did the Marshall Plan contribute to the division of Europe between 1947 and 1949?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use Marshall Plan data, Soviet responses (Molotov) and two historians; compare interpretations; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use Marshall Plan data, Soviet responses (Molotov) and two historians; compare interpretations; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: "Containment was a successful policy for the USA between 1947 and 1962." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Containment largely succeeded in Europe, but its record in Asia and Latin America was mixed and costly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it preserved West Berlin, Western Europe and South Korea; Soviet missiles were removed from Cuba. Arguments against: the USA failed to stop communist victories in China (1949) and Cuba (1959); Korea ended in stalemate with huge loss of life. Supported judgement: Containment largely succeeded in Europe, but its record in Asia and Latin America was mixed and costly. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Who won the space race?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the arms race, the space race and Cold War propaganda. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed question Improved: "How did the launch of Sputnik in 1957 influence US education and science policy?"

Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.
